prize_parts.citation: for the development of targeted protein degradation, using small molecules to direct the ubiquitin-proteasome system against chosen proteins

statement.case_for: Targeted protein degradation turns the ubiquitin-proteasome machinery into a programmable chemical tool. Heterobifunctional PROTACs (Crews and Deshaies) and molecular glues explained mechanistically through cereblon (Handa) are two sides of one idea, which is to induce proximity between an E3 ligase and a protein chosen by the chemist. The chemical content is real: linker and ligand design, ternary-complex cooperativity and the mechanistic explanation of thalidomide-class drugs. It also gives biochemists a new experimental way to remove a protein acutely, which complements genetic knockouts and knockdowns. It is the only shortlisted candidate that eight of eight members ranked, and two members placed it first. Its support is broad rather than a first-place plurality of one field, which I weigh more than any single member's enthusiasm. The mechanism has been independently confirmed in many laboratories, and degraders are in clinical development.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity. As far as the committee can establish, no PROTAC has yet been approved, so the therapeutic argument rests on clinical-stage evidence. A second problem is attribution. The shortlist credits eight people, and a three-person cut that leaves out Ciulli (VHL ligands, structural work that made the approach drug-like), Gray, Sakamoto, Ito and Kim is contestable. A prize that joins PROTAC design with the cereblon mechanism may also look like two discoveries awkwardly merged. If clinical validation stalls over the next few years, or if resistance mechanisms prove severe, the committee may regret acting early.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranked proton-coupled electron transfer (B025) first, as a unifying physical principle in respiration, photosynthesis and electrocatalysis with decades of confirmation, and placed B063 second, noting its credit is spread over too many names and its clinical case is still maturing.
responses.response: I agree with his maturity and attribution reservations on B063, and I do not dismiss them. But PCET is a concept that was built up over decades in many hands, and the shortlist leaves open whether Mayer, Hammes-Schiffer, Nocera and Meyer form a single discovery with a clean citation. Only he ranked it, so its support is narrow. B063 has the more definable claim, since PROTAC conception plus the cereblon mechanism can be cited together, and the cut to Crews, Deshaies and Handa is at least a principled one. Maturity is the one point where his case is stronger than mine, and I accept that it counts against timing for B063, not against its merit. I would still ask him whether he can support B063 if B025 does not gain traction.

responses.point: Aqvist ranked prime editing (B061) first as a protein-engineering and RNA-chemistry invention that is conceptually distinct from CRISPR and fits best as a Liu-centred award, and he ranked ionizable lipid nanoparticles (B035) second, while placing B063 fifth.
responses.response: His argument for Liu's central role is sound, and I ranked base editing in my own opening list, so I take it seriously. My reservation is timing. Prime editing is about seven years old, with only early clinical use, and the 2020 CRISPR prize makes the novelty argument harder. Base editing (B068) and prime editing (B061) are also so close that the committee should not split Liu's work artificially, and I think that should be resolved before either is advanced. On B035 we agree it deserves serious consideration. Where I differ is that I think the maturity case is stronger for lipid nanoparticles than for editing, so I would put B035 ahead of both, with B063 first only because I see a cleaner chemistry story in it.

responses.point: Sparr ranked ionizable lipid nanoparticles (B035) first as physical chemistry of lipid assembly with global clinical impact, proposed a Cullis, Hope and Madden core, and ranked B063 fourth.
responses.response: I agree with her on merit and on the point that the 2023 Medicine prize recognised the nucleoside-modified cargo, not the carrier. I disagree on one point. Her Vancouver trio leaves out Anderson, and Anderson's combinatorial lipidoid work is regarded as an independent route to the same delivery chemistry, so the pure Vancouver attribution is open to challenge. I also find the Vancouver-Boston patent history harder to settle than the PROTAC history, where the concept and mechanism papers are not contested in priority. So I put it second, not first, but I would not oppose it if the committee prefers it.

responses.point: Linke, as chair, ranked massively parallel sequencing (B031) first, arguing that sequencing-by-synthesis chemistry is a genuinely chemical invention best credited to Balasubramanian and Klenerman, and he placed B063 fourth.
responses.response: I accept the chemistry argument for reversible terminators and the two-person cut is the cleaner one. But I rank B031 below B063 because the question of fit remains: much of its impact is as an enabling platform for genomics, and the chemistry-versus-biology boundary will be argued over. His point about Sanger sequencing is fair and makes novelty a harder case. I would like to hear how he weighs the competing claims of Ju and Mayer when only two names are allowed.

uncertainties: Whether PROTACs and molecular glues should be recognised as one discovery or whether the citation should be narrowed to one of them
Whether the lack of an approved PROTAC drug makes the prize premature, and what clinical milestones the committee would regard as sufficient
Whether omitting Ciulli, Gray and Sakamoto is defensible, or whether a different three-person cut is fairer
Whether B035 or B068 should take precedence over B063 if the committee weighs maturity above conceptual breadth
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My work on nucleotide metabolism and replication fidelity does not overlap directly with any shortlisted candidate, and I have no documented collaboration with any credited person. I note only that my field is biochemistry and medical chemistry, and that I am a biologist-classified academician with possible bias toward chemical-biology candidates.
